title: Iran resumes attacks on Bahrain as markets brace for Nvidia week
dek: US markets are closed for the weekend, but Iran's renewed strikes on Bahrain add an oil-price risk when futures reopen Sunday evening. The week ahead brings Fed Chair Warsh on Monday, retail sales and Nvidia's results Tuesday, and Anthropic's Nasdaq debut Thursday, with the 10-year yield above 5%.
quick: Sunday edition: no trading today. Stock futures reopen at 6 p.m. ET; on Friday the S&P 500 fell 0.4% but gained 2.5% for the week.
Bahrain said it intercepted several Iranian aerial attacks Sunday, after Iran struck a US radar site there Friday, the first known attack on Bahrain in two months.
Pressure is building on Nvidia's board: two large investors asked it to consider bringing Jensen Huang back, and the company reports Tuesday after the close.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks Monday around noon ET; futures price a December rate hike as close to certain, with the 10-year yield near 5.14%.
President Trump is set to meet China's Xi and Russia's Putin in China this week, with US tech executives also expected for a summit in Shenzhen.
Anthropic plans to price its IPO Wednesday and start trading on Nasdaq Thursday; gold, Bitcoin and oil all ended last week lower.

blocks.head: Iran renews attacks on Bahrain, raising oil risk
blocks.what: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Friday they destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain, in retaliation for a US airstrike on a communications tower near the Strait of Hormuz, according to the Guardian; the US said it intercepted the drone strike, the first known attack on Bahrain in two months, the Wall Street Journal reported. On Sunday, Bahrain's military said its air defenses intercepted several more Iranian aerial attacks, while Tehran said it had targeted a US base, CNBC and the Journal reported. The Journal also reported that US officials estimate Iran still has up to 2,500 missiles, a figure that has factored into administration discussions about whether to resume strikes.
blocks.why: Oil had fallen for two straight weeks on expectations of a fourth-quarter supply surplus, so renewed Gulf attacks could push crude and energy stocks higher when trading reopens, and weigh on airlines. A flight to safety could also support Treasuries and the dollar, though inflation worries have been pushing yields the other way.
blocks.watch: Brent and US crude futures when they reopen Sunday evening, and any US military response.

blocks.head: Nvidia's board faces pressure before Tuesday's results
blocks.what: Two Nvidia investors holding about $2.13 billion of stock as of June 30 urged the board to run a deliberate search for a permanent CEO and to consider a potential return of Jensen Huang, CNBC reported Saturday. Elon Musk and other tech executives signed a petition calling for Huang's reinstatement, TechCrunch reported, and the NYT and WSJ described a wave of tech leaders defending him. The board told CNBC it has not yet chosen a search firm. Nvidia closed Friday below $4 trillion in market value for the first time since July 2025 after six straight weekly declines.
blocks.why: Nvidia is the largest weight in the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq, so its report and any leadership news will move the indexes and chip stocks such as AMD, Broadcom and Intel. Analysts expect revenue near $108.8 billion versus company guidance of $108 billion.
blocks.watch: Tuesday's outlook and comments from interim CEO Colette Kress, and any board statement on succession.

blocks.head: Warsh and retail sales test the Fed hike bets
blocks.what: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks Monday around noon ET, his first scheduled remarks since October consumer prices rose 0.4% versus a 0.3% forecast and producer prices rose 6.5% from a year earlier. Several Fed presidents said last week that more rate increases look appropriate. Tuesday brings October retail sales, which economists polled by Newsquawk expect to rise 0.2% after 0.8% in September. Separately, a Fed survey released Friday found market contacts now see AI-related risks as the biggest threat to the financial system, CNBC reported.
blocks.why: Fed funds futures already price a December hike as close to certain. Any hint from Warsh of a half-point move, or strong spending data, would likely push short-term yields and the dollar higher and weigh on rate-sensitive stocks such as small caps and homebuilders.
blocks.watch: Whether Warsh discusses the size of a December move or the path into January.

blocks.head: Trump to meet Xi and Putin in China
blocks.what: The White House said President Trump will hold a joint meeting with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin in China this week, with reducing nuclear weapons on the agenda, the BBC and NYT reported. The NYT said the Iran war will also be discussed, but not Russia's war in Ukraine or the Nvidia scandal. US tech executives are expected at a summit in Shenzhen where a stalled trade war and expanding export controls are on the agenda, according to the NYT. Ahead of the talks, Chinese and US officials discussed tariffs and farm trade; Beijing has said carrying out a $60 billion tariff-reduction deal is a precondition for more US farm purchases, CNBC reported.
blocks.why: Outcomes on tariffs and chip export rules matter for chipmakers' China sales, farm commodities such as soybeans, China-exposed US companies, and the yuan.
blocks.watch: Any tariff or farm-purchase announcements and whether export controls come up despite official guidance.

blocks.head: Anthropic's IPO arrives midweek
blocks.what: Anthropic expects to price its initial public offering on or about Wednesday and begin trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday, with an indicated range of $70 to $78 a share for about 825 million shares. The Wall Street Journal reported the company is targeting a valuation of roughly $1.33 trillion or more, and that CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon he hopes the offering will underpromise and overdeliver. The NYT reported banks are pitching it as potentially the largest IPO ever.
blocks.why: An offering this size can pull money from other holdings as funds make room, and its reception will be read as a gauge of investor appetite for AI after the Nvidia shock.
blocks.watch: Whether the price range is raised or the deal is priced above it Wednesday night.

blocks.head: Washington fallout: Lutnick scrutiny and the FAA outage
blocks.what: The NYT reported that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick pushed to weaken pending chip-export rules affecting Southeast Asian data centers, some of which are clients of his former firm; Sen. Richard Blumenthal called for his resignation, and CNBC reported Lutnick will testify before the Senate Banking Committee. On Friday's nationwide flight ground stop, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said it followed contractor work on an older communications system managed by L3Harris, including replacing copper wire with fiber at a remote FAA site, CNBC and The Verge reported; the FAA has said a definitive root cause has not been established. Democrats, who won control of both chambers in the midterms and take over in January, pushed back on Duffy's request for $50 billion to upgrade air traffic systems, the NYT reported.
blocks.why: Tighter or looser export rules would change the outlook for chip sales routed through Southeast Asia. L3Harris shares and airline stocks may react Monday to the outage findings and weekend cancellation costs.
blocks.watch: The date of Lutnick's testimony and any new Commerce entity-list actions.

blocks.text: Asia

Asian markets reopen Sunday evening US time. On Friday, Japan's Nikkei 225 rose about 0.5% to 61,142, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell about 1.5% and Shanghai slipped 0.6% as AI-linked shares in the region came under pressure from the Nvidia news. This week the region hosts back-to-back summits in China, the Philippines and Cambodia, the Guardian reported, and China's monthly activity data is due.
Europe

Europe's Stoxx 600 closed essentially flat Friday at 664.14, a record, and gained about 2.4% for the week as insurers and oil companies offset weaker chipmakers. London's FTSE 100 rose 0.4% to 10,903, and Germany's DAX was little changed. UK inflation and jobs reports are due this week.
Currencies

The dollar index ended the week near 103.4, close to a 19-month high, after its biggest weekly gain since September as Fed hike bets grew. The yen sits at about 159.7 per dollar, just under the 160 level it briefly touched Thursday; Japan's finance minister has said the government will respond appropriately to sharp moves, and Tokyo spent 15.4 trillion yen supporting the currency in late July. The euro is about $1.102, the pound about $1.322, and the yuan about 6.67 per dollar. Any summit progress on trade could affect the yuan, while a hawkish Warsh would tend to lift the dollar further.

US markets are closed today; the live table below shows Friday's closing levels. Stock index futures reopen at 6 p.m. ET, and the first test will be how oil and futures absorb Iran's weekend attacks on Bahrain. On Friday the S&P 500 fell 0.4% and the Nasdaq Composite 0.9%, while the Dow edged up 0.1%, as chip stocks sold off and the 10-year yield rose back above 5%. The VIX volatility gauge ended near 19.3.

For the week, the S&P 500 gained 2.5%, its first winning week since early October, recovering part of the sharp AI-driven selloff of November 5. Nvidia's results Tuesday are the week's biggest single-stock event.

The 10-year Treasury yield ended Friday near 5.14%, after touching 5.17% intraday, and the 30-year closed near 5.47%. The 2-year yield dipped to about 4.85%. That leaves the 10-year about 29 basis points above the 2-year, a steeper curve that reflects investors demanding more to hold long-term debt while inflation runs hot.

The Fed's policy range is 3.75% to 4.00%, and its next meeting is December 8 to 9. Fed funds futures tracked by CME Group's FedWatch tool price a December hike as nearly certain, mostly a quarter point with a smaller chance of a half point, and markets lean toward another increase in January, according to Reuters. Boston's Susan Collins and Philadelphia's Anna Paulson said last week further tightening looks appropriate, and Chicago's Austan Goolsbee called October's consumer price report borderline disturbing. Governor Christopher Waller has raised the possibility of a half-point move. Wednesday's minutes cover the October meeting, when the Fed held rates steady, and predate the hot October inflation reports.
Fed speakers this week

items: Monday: Governor Michael Barr (early morning ET), New York's John Williams (about 9:05 a.m. ET), Chair Kevin Warsh (about noon ET).
Tuesday: St. Louis's Alberto Musalem, Governor Christopher Waller, Cleveland's Beth Hammack, and Williams again in the afternoon.
Wednesday: Barr, Williams and Minneapolis's Neel Kashkari, plus the October minutes at 2 p.m. ET.
Thursday: Hammack, Goolsbee, Barr, Richmond's Tom Barkin and Paulson.
Friday: Waller and Governor Lisa Cook.

blocks.text: Technology was the weakest S&P 500 sector Friday, with the sector fund down about 2% as chip stocks sold off; consumer discretionary, industrials and materials also slipped. Defensive and value groups led: consumer staples rose about 1.4%, communication services about 1.1%, energy about 1% and financials about 0.8%, with health care and utilities each up roughly 0.5%. The pattern fit a week of money rotating out of AI names toward steadier businesses. Berkshire Hathaway closed at a record high for a fourth straight session, CNBC reported.
Names to watch Monday

items: Nvidia: board pressure over Huang's possible return and Tuesday's results; the stock has fallen six weeks in a row.
AMD, Broadcom, Intel: fell hard Friday as the 'rivals benefit' trade unwound; they will trade off Nvidia headlines.
Energy producers and airlines: opposite exposure to any oil jump from the Bahrain attacks; airlines also carry ground-stop costs.
L3Harris: named by the Transportation secretary in connection with Friday's FAA outage.
Home Depot: reports Tuesday before the open, the first of the big retailers this week.

blocks.text: Oil

Brent settled near $95.84 a barrel Friday and US crude just under $89, with US crude down about 2.5% for its second straight weekly decline. The International Energy Agency expects a fourth-quarter supply surplus of about 1.7 million barrels a day, the first since the Iran war began in February. The weekend's Iranian attacks on Bahrain cut against that calmer picture and are the main risk when futures reopen.
Gold

Gold settled near $3,888 an ounce, down about 4% for the week and near its lowest level in about 13 months, as higher Treasury yields and a stronger dollar raised the cost of holding a metal that pays no interest.
Crypto

Bitcoin was trading near $65,500 early Sunday, according to the app's quote feed, down from about $67,200 on Saturday morning, and Ether was near $1,830. US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw about $1.07 billion of outflows from November 9 to 13, after $1.28 billion the week before, according to Farside data. Rising rate-hike expectations and the coming Anthropic IPO, which could draw speculative money, have weighed on the asset class.
There are no US economic releases, Fed speakers or market sessions today. Futures reopen at 6 p.m. ET. The first items that matter come Monday and Tuesday:

items: Monday 8:30 a.m. ET: New York Fed's Empire State manufacturing index; forecast 17.6 after 25.5.
Monday about noon ET: Fed Chair Warsh speaks; the most important event of the day for rates.
Tuesday 8:30 a.m. ET: October retail sales, forecast up 0.2% after 0.8%, and the 'core' measure up 0.4% after 0.9%; import prices seen up 0.7%.
Tuesday 9:15 a.m. ET: industrial production, forecast up 0.1% after 0.7%.

blocks.text: No major companies report this weekend. These are the week's key reports, by date as listed in company calendars and earnings previews.

rows: Analysts expect about $3.84 a share on $42.8 billion revenue; housing-related spending with mortgage rates above 7%.
Consensus near $108.8 billion revenue and $2.47 a share vs. $108 billion guidance; next-quarter outlook and leadership comments.
Home improvement demand and its full-year outlook.
Analysts expect about 63 cents a share on $187.2 billion revenue; whether it raises its full-year outlook.

blocks.text: It is a crowded week for the AI trade, inflation and the Fed, now with added geopolitical risk. Monday brings the Empire State survey and Chair Warsh. Tuesday is the biggest day: retail sales and industrial production in the morning, Home Depot before the open and Nvidia after the close. Wednesday has housing starts, the Fed's October minutes, Lowe's and Target, and Anthropic's expected IPO pricing. Thursday brings Anthropic's first trade on Nasdaq, Walmart, weekly jobless claims (forecast 199,000), the Philly Fed survey and five Fed speakers. Friday ends with the revised University of Michigan consumer sentiment and inflation expectations survey and Waller. Running through it all are the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting in China and the Iran-Bahrain flare-up. With the 10-year near 5.14% and a December hike largely priced in, strong spending data or hawkish Fed comments would test that pricing, while Nvidia's guidance and Anthropic's debut will show how much appetite remains for AI stocks.

bottom_line: Markets enter the week after an S&P 500 weekly gain but with chip stocks under pressure, yields above 5% and a December Fed hike largely priced in. Iran's weekend attacks on Bahrain add an oil-price risk to a schedule already packed with Warsh, retail sales, Nvidia and the Anthropic IPO.
